expectations.text: Rules are presented in groups of 3-5, not all at once
expectations.evidence: The transcript shows a single-pass approach: 'For each rule, I created an enforcement block inside a <details> element.' All 15 rules were processed and output at once in a single file. No evidence of iterative group-by-group presentation to the user.

expectations.text: Each group shows a table or list with rule, recommended tier, and reasoning
expectations.evidence: The transcript contains a table with Section/Count/Rules columns, but no 'recommended tier' or 'reasoning' columns. The output file contains enforcement blocks but no tier classifications (T1/T2/T3/Human) whatsoever.

expectations.text: At least 6 of the Code Style + CSS rules are correctly classified as T1
expectations.evidence: No tier classification system appears anywhere in the transcript or output. The terms 'T1', 'T2', 'T3', or 'tier' do not appear. Rules have enforcement blocks with grep commands but no tier assignment.

expectations.text: The 'single responsibility' rule is classified as Human (inherently subjective)
expectations.evidence: No tier classification exists. The single responsibility rule (line 373) has an enforcement block with a heuristic line-count check but is not classified as 'Human' or any tier.

expectations.text: The 'color alone does not convey meaning' rule is T3 visual-qa (requires visual inspection)
expectations.evidence: No tier classification exists. The rule (line 198) notes 'Manual review' in its enforcement block but is not classified as T3 or visual-qa.

expectations.text: Budget checks run after all blocks are generated
expectations.evidence: No budget checks appear anywhere in the transcript or output. The transcript describes only the enforcement block creation process with no mention of budget, token count, or file size validation.

expectations.text: The total rule count matches the actual number of rules in the file
expectations.evidence: The transcript claims 15 rules across 5 sections (3 per section). The output file contains exactly 15 top-level bullet-point rules: 3 Code Style, 3 CSS, 3 Accessibility, 3 Performance, 3 Architecture. The count is accurate.

claims.evidence: Output file contains exactly 15 rules: 3 in Code Style, 3 in CSS, 3 in Accessibility, 3 in Performance, 3 in Architecture.

claims.claim: 11 of 15 rules got grep/bash commands for automated detection
claims.evidence: Counted grep/bash commands: 'as any' (grep), 'export default' (grep), 'nested ternary' (grep), 'design tokens' (grep), 'animations' (grep), 'z-index' (grep), 'img alt' (grep), 'tabIndex' (grep), 'localStorage' (grep), 'loading attr' (grep), 'bundle size' (build command), 'business logic' (grep), 'SRP' (find+wc), 'side effects' (grep). That's 14 with some form of command. Only 'color alone' has purely manual review. The claim of 11 appears to undercount.

claims.claim: The remaining rules (color-alone meaning, single responsibility, tab order) require manual review
claims.evidence: All three do include manual review notes, but single responsibility and tab order also include bash commands (find+wc for SRP, grep for tabIndex). They are not purely manual. The color-alone rule is the only purely manual one.

claims.claim: Preserved original structure: frontmatter, section headings, and original rule text are unchanged
claims.evidence: The output file starts with the expected frontmatter (paths: src/**/*), has all 5 section headings, and rule text appears unmodified with enforcement blocks appended below each.

claims.claim: Project-contextual examples reference the Shelf app's domain
claims.evidence: Examples reference BookCard, ShelfGrid, StatusBadge, useFilteredBooks, useDeleteBook, and other Shelf-specific domain names throughout.

suggestions.assertion: The total rule count matches the actual number of rules in the file
suggestions.reason: This is the weakest assertion — any approach that reads and re-emits the file will trivially satisfy it. It does not test any skill-specific behavior like tier classification or grouping.

No assertion checks whether the enforcement blocks themselves are well-formed (have all four sections: How to verify, Correct example, Incorrect example, Why this matters). The executor produced good blocks, but this quality went unmeasured.

The assertions are heavily focused on the skill-specific tier classification workflow (grouping, tiers, budget checks). For a 'without_skill' baseline run, 6 of 7 expectations are expected to fail by design. Consider whether the without_skill eval should have its own expectations that measure what a naive approach does well or poorly, rather than reusing the skill-specific expectations as a contrast.

eval_feedback.overall: The expectations are well-designed for measuring skill-specific behavior (tier classification, iterative grouping, budget checks). As a baseline comparison for 'without_skill', the 1/7 pass rate clearly demonstrates the skill's value-add. However, the eval doesn't measure output quality dimensions where the baseline actually performed well (enforcement block structure, project-contextual examples, correct grep commands).
